reader.title: Disruption of the Ship Island Park picnic meeting
bases: Both versions describe white men at a Black Republican picnic intervening so a Black Democratic speaker could be heard, which the Chicago Tribune called intimidation and seizure of the meeting; no killing, injury or property damage is reported (A1, A3).

Every account derives from one Natchez Democrat report, summarized by the Chicago Tribune (A1, reprinted in A2) and quoted by the Watertown Republican (A3); no independent local or Black-press report was found.

summary.text: The disruption of the Ship Island Park picnic meeting was an incident in August 1880 in which white men at a Black Republican picnic at Ship Island Park, near Vicksburg, Mississippi, intervened on behalf of a Black Democratic speaker.
No one was reported hurt, but Northern Republican papers took up the case as an example of Southern denial of free speech.

The Natchez Democrat complained that "the John Lynch radicals" were turning "colored picnics" into political meetings, and the Ship Island Park gathering, held a few days before 13 August, was one of these.
After John R. Lynch and a man named Harris spoke, a Black man named Cox, "hired by the Democrats" in the Tribune's words, insisted on replying in behalf of Chalmers.
The crowd shouted that it did not want to hear any Democrat.

According to the Chicago Tribune, the whites "had prepared for this" and were present in such numbers that they intimidated the Black attendees, took possession of the meeting and stopped Republican speech-making.
The Democrat's own words, quoted by the Watertown Republican, said only that Cox "would doubtless have been hooted down had it not been for the efforts of white men on the ground."
No report of injuries or arrests appears in the coverage.

The Natchez Democrat reported the meeting to argue that Black Republicans were as intolerant of opposing speech as Southern whites were said to be, and urged that such "old time tricks" be "sternly rebuked."

The Chicago Daily Tribune turned the item against it on 13 August in an editorial headed "'Free Speech' at the South," calling Chalmers "the chief of Mississippi bulldozers," and the Omaha Daily Bee reprinted that editorial on 18 August.
On 25 August the Watertown Republican of Wisconsin quoted the Democrat at length and called it a "Bourbon organ."

Because the Watertown paper quoted the Democrat directly while the Tribune paraphrased it, the Watertown text is closer to the original, though that report came from the paper that defended the white men's role.

accounts.label: Natchez Democrat (as quoted)
accounts.gist: Lynch's supporters turned a 'colored picnic' into a radical political meeting and would have hooted down Cox but for the efforts of white men on the ground; the audience had a right to answer Lynch.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune editorial
accounts.gist: The whites had prepared for the Black audience's refusal to hear Cox and were present in such numbers that they intimidated the Black people, took possession of the meeting and stopped Republican speech-making.

framing.detail: Chicago Tribune editorial '"Free Speech" at the South' cited the picnic beside a Texas case as Democrats' claim to interrupt Republican meetings, calling Chalmers 'the chief of Mississippi bulldozers'.
The Watertown Republican's 'Free Speech North and South' quoted the Natchez Democrat at length and called it a 'Bourbon organ' whose idea of free speech would strike Northern readers as peculiar.
The Natchez Democrat, as quoted, cast the picnic as a radical trick, defended Cox's hearing and said such 'old time tricks' must be 'sternly rebuked'.

versions.value: Whites intimidated the Black attendees, took possession of the meeting and stopped Republican speech-making
White men's efforts only kept Cox from being hooted down; the Democrat does not say Republican speaking was stopped

conflicts.note: Both versions trace to the same Natchez Democrat report; the Tribune's is a hostile paraphrase, while the Watertown Republican quotes the Democrat's words directly, so A3 is closer to the original, though it too comes only from the side that defended the white men's role.
